parts: Sunday, September third, nineteen sixty-seven. Ten minutes to five in the morning.
Across Sweden, the cars, buses and trucks still on the road come to a stop.
Then the drivers cross to the other side of the road.
Why would a whole country do this?
Until that morning, Swedish traffic kept to the left.
Wikipedia says every neighboring country drove on the right, and about five million vehicles crossed those borders each year.
It adds that more than nine in ten Swedes drove cars with the steering wheel on the left.
Our reading: in left-hand traffic, that put the driver at the curb, with a poor view when passing.
In nineteen fifty-five, Sweden held a vote on the change.
Eighty-three percent said no.
Parliament approved the switch anyway, in May nineteen sixty-three.
Wikipedia says cars had tripled, to one and a half million, and were expected to keep growing.
Our reading: waiting would only make it harder.
Then came four years of preparation, run by a special commission.
Households received a pamphlet explaining the change.
The campaign logo, an H, appeared on milk cartons and even on underwear.
A pop song, "Keep to the right, Svensson," became a hit.
About three hundred fifty thousand road signs had to be removed or replaced.
Wikipedia says more than a thousand new buses had doors on the right, and about eight thousand older ones were modified.
Extra traffic signals waited wrapped in black plastic until that morning.
Then came the night. Non-essential traffic was banned from one to six in the morning.
At ten to five, the traffic on the road stopped.
The podcast Ninety-nine Percent Invisible says a horn sounded in Stockholm, then a loudspeaker said it was time to change over.
Drivers crossed over, and waited ten minutes.
At five o'clock, traffic moved off again, slowly, on the right.
That day, one hundred fifty-seven accidents were reported, and few were serious.
The next Monday had one hundred twenty-five, fewer than on earlier Mondays.
Wikipedia says experts pointed to extra caution.
But the gains faded, it adds. By nineteen sixty-nine, accident rates were back to where they began.
Not everyone had wanted the change.
Most voters had said no in nineteen fifty-five, and the switch went ahead anyway.
Our reading: the day went smoothly because it was planned for years.
Even a well-planned system can hide a tiny fault.
In machines, we call them bugs.
Where does that word come from?
